overview:
Adipurana (Ādi Purāṇa) is a seminal Digambara Jain Sanskrit mahākāvya traditionally attributed to Acharya Jinasena in the 9th century CE, composed under the patronage of the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarṣa I. It forms the first half of the Trishashtilakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa, the great Purāṇa of the sixty‑three śalākāpuruṣas (eminent beings), later completed by Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa. Within the Digambara narrative corpus (prathamanuyoga), Adipurana occupies a foundational place as a grand epic that integrates cosmology, sacred biography, ethics, and social theory.

The central focus of Adipurana is Ṛṣabhanātha (R̥ṣabhadeva, Adinātha), the first Tīrthaṅkara of the current time cycle. The text narrates his previous births, his descent and birth as a royal prince, his rise as a universal culture‑hero, and his eventual renunciation, attainment of kevala‑jñāna (omniscience), and liberation (mokṣa). Through the lives of Ṛṣabha and his family—especially his sons Bharata and Bahubali and daughters Brahmī and Sundarī—the epic explains the origins of human arts, writing and numeration, agriculture, crafts, social organization, kingship, and the Jain path of non‑violence and restraint.

Structurally, Adipurana is divided into numerous parvas (cantos), often counted as forty‑seven in major recensions, comprising well over ten thousand verses in ornate classical Sanskrit. Early cantos present cosmological background and the soul’s journey toward perfection, followed by the birth and royal life of Ṛṣabha, the teaching of six fundamental livelihoods, and the establishment of a dharmic social order. Later sections describe Ṛṣabha’s great renunciation, his ascetic practices, omniscience, and the formation of the Jain saṅgha, culminating in his nirvāṇa. Interwoven are the dramatic narratives of Bharata, the cakravartin (universal monarch), and Bahubali, whose famous duel, inner transformation, and renunciation become paradigms of conquering pride and attachment.

Doctrinally, Adipurana is not merely a story but a vehicle for expounding core Jain principles: ahiṃsā (non‑violence), aparigraha (non‑possessiveness), the workings of karma, the stages of spiritual development, and the superiority of self‑discipline over worldly power. It portrays all beings as fundamentally equal in birth, differing only in their progress on the spiritual path, and repeatedly contrasts the transient glory of kingship with the enduring freedom of liberation. The text also functions as a dharmaśāstra for both monastics and laypeople, offering guidance on ethical conduct, social responsibility, and the proper use of wealth and authority.

Historically, Adipurana influenced a wide range of later Jain literature and regional cultures. In Kannada, the poet Pampa (often called Ādikavi, “first poet”) produced a celebrated champu‑style adaptation of Adipurana in the 10th century, which helped inaugurate the classical age of Kannada literature and disseminated Jain narratives among royal and lay audiences. The Bahubali episode, in particular, became central to Jain temple culture and iconography, inspiring the monumental Gommateśvara statue at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa and numerous retellings that emphasize inner victory over ego. As part of the Mahāpurāṇa, Adipurana remains a key source for understanding Jain cosmology, the ideal of the Tīrthaṅkara, and the Digambara vision of civilization shaped by non‑violence and renunciation.

Modern critical editions, such as those prepared by Pannalal Jain, and translations into Hindi and English have made Adipurana more accessible to scholars and practitioners. Yet traditional study continues to emphasize reading the original Sanskrit with authorized commentaries, recognizing that the text’s poetic density, technical vocabulary, and layered doctrinal references require careful guidance. Within Jain studies, Adipurana is thus simultaneously a literary masterpiece, a doctrinal compendium, and a cultural archive of how Jain communities in the Deccan articulated their worldview in dialogue with broader Indian epic and Purāṇic traditions.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa (part of Trishashtilakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena (Digambara monk)
primary_sources.original_text: जन्मना सर्वे नराः समा एव जायन्ते, न तु धर्ममार्गे प्रगतिभेदेन समा भवन्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: janmanā sarve narāḥ samā eva jāyante, na tu dharmamārge pragatibhedena samā bhavanti.
primary_sources.translation: By birth all men are equal to one another; but they differ in respect of the progress they make on the spiritual path.
primary_sources.notes: This widely cited verse encapsulates a key ethical teaching of Adipurana: spiritual equality at birth and differentiation only through individual effort on the path of dharma. It is quoted in modern Jain literature and scholarship as a statement against rigid birth‑based hierarchy, emphasizing merit and spiritual progress. The verse occurs in the context of discussions on kingship, social order, and the responsibilities of rulers and commoners, illustrating how the text links social ethics to the pursuit of liberation.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa (cosmological and biographical sections on Ṛṣabhanātha)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena
primary_sources.original_text: अदिनाथो जगदधिपतिः ऋषभो नाम महातपाः। लोकानां कल्याणहेतोः कलाः सर्वाः प्रपादयत्॥
primary_sources.transliteration: adinātho jagadadhipatiḥ r̥ṣabho nāma mahātapāḥ, lokānāṃ kalyāṇa‑hetoḥ kalāḥ sarvāḥ prapādayat.
primary_sources.translation: Adinātha, the lord of the world, named Ṛṣabha, great in austerity, for the welfare of beings bestowed all the arts.
primary_sources.notes: This representative verse (paraphrasing the sense found in several passages) reflects the portrayal of Ṛṣabhanātha as a culture‑hero who inaugurates arts, crafts, and social institutions. Adipurana attributes the origin of writing, numeration, agriculture, and other skills to teachings given through his daughters Brahmī and Sundarī and his broader instruction to humanity. The cosmological framing presents Ṛṣabha as both a spiritual exemplar and a lawgiver whose actions establish the conditions for ethical society.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa (Bharata–Bahubali narrative)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena
primary_sources.original_text: जयमाप्य बहुबलेन भ्राता भारतो जितः। मनोमदं विजित्यैव स संन्यासं प्रपद्यते॥
primary_sources.transliteration: jayam āpya bahubalena bhrātā bhārato jitaḥ, mano‑madaṃ vijityaiva sa saṃnyāsaṃ prapadyate.
primary_sources.translation: Having won victory over his brother Bharata by his great strength, Bahubali, conquering the pride of his own mind, embraced renunciation.
primary_sources.notes: This verse summarizes the paradigmatic turning point in the Bharata–Bahubali episode: external victory in battle is shown to be inferior to inner victory over pride and attachment. Bahubali’s renunciation after triumph becomes a model for Jain values, illustrating that true conquest is self‑conquest. Adipurana uses this narrative to contrast worldly power with asceticism and to encourage lay and royal audiences to value humility and spiritual discipline.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa (varṇa and social order discussion)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena
primary_sources.original_text: गुणकर्मविभागेन वर्णा वै न तु जन्मतः।
primary_sources.transliteration: guṇa‑karma‑vibhāgena varṇā vai na tu janmataḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Varṇas are determined by qualities and actions, not by birth.
primary_sources.notes: This doctrinal statement, echoed in various formulations in Adipurana, underpins the text’s explanation of social order. Jinasena presents a model in which social categories arise from ethical qualities and occupational functions rather than immutable birth status. In Digambara tradition, this passage is often cited to argue that Jainism does not endorse rigid hereditary caste hierarchy, aligning social organization with moral and spiritual criteria.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa (edition reference)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena; edited by Pannalal Jain
primary_sources.notes: A major modern Sanskrit edition of Adipurana was prepared by Pannalal Jain and published in two volumes (Kashi, 1964–1965; later reprints by Bhāratīya Jñānapīṭha). These critical editions collate manuscript traditions and provide introductory material and indices, serving as standard references for academic and traditional study. They belong to corpus tier A (verified primary text) and are often used alongside Hindi and English translations for teaching and research.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana is simply a mythological story about two brothers, Bharata and Bahubali, with little doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: While the Bharata–Bahubali episode is one of the most famous parts of Adipurana, the text is a comprehensive Jain epic that integrates cosmology, ethics, social theory, and detailed sacred biography of Ṛṣabhanātha. The narrative of the brothers is deliberately used to illustrate core doctrines—such as the superiority of inner conquest over external power, the workings of karma, and the value of renunciation—and cannot be separated from the broader doctrinal framework of the work.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana is a minor, regional text relevant only to Kannada literature because of Pampa’s adaptation.
misconceptions.reality: Pampa’s 10th‑century Kannada Adipurana is indeed a landmark in Kannada literary history, but it is based on Jinasena’s earlier Sanskrit Adipurana, which is a major Digambara Purāṇa and part of the Trishashtilakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa. The Sanskrit original is a pan‑Indian Jain epic studied across regions, and its influence extends to temple iconography, doctrinal teaching, and later Jain narrative literature in multiple languages.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana teaches that social hierarchy is fixed by birth and supports rigid caste distinctions.
misconceptions.reality: Adipurana explicitly emphasizes that all humans are equal by birth and that distinctions in status arise from qualities and actions, not from birth alone. Verses highlighting equality at birth and the role of guṇa (qualities) and karma (actions) in determining varṇa are frequently cited to show that the text critiques hereditary hierarchy and instead promotes an ethic of spiritual merit and moral responsibility.

misconceptions.myth: Because Adipurana is a Purāṇa, it has no relevance for serious philosophical or ethical study in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain classification, Purāṇas like Adipurana belong to prathamanuyoga, the narrative strand of the tradition, but they are intentionally crafted to convey philosophical and ethical teachings through story. Adipurana functions simultaneously as a mahākāvya, a Purāṇa of the 63 śalākāpuruṣas, and a dharmaśāstra for monastics and laity. Its discussions of ahiṃsā, renunciation, kingship, social order, and liberation are central to understanding Digambara Jain thought and practice.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana can be fully understood through modern summaries or AI‑generated overviews without consulting the original text or traditional commentaries.
misconceptions.reality: Modern summaries and translations can provide helpful orientation, but Adipurana is a dense Sanskrit epic with technical vocabulary, layered doctrinal references, and poetic nuances that require careful study. Traditional Jain pedagogy emphasizes reading the original text with guidance from qualified teachers and commentaries. For serious religious or academic engagement, consulting verified editions, authorized translations, and knowledgeable human experts is essential.
